overview: NiSource is an energy holding company under the Public Utility Holding Company Act of 2005 whose principal subsidiaries are fully regulated natural gas and electric utilities serving approximately 3.8 million customers across six states (Ohio, Pennsylvania, Virginia, Kentucky, Maryland and Indiana). Its two reportable segments are Columbia Operations (natural gas distribution in five eastern/mid-Atlantic states) and NIPSCO Operations (combined gas and electric utility in northern Indiana). NiSource has become a focal point of the AI/data-center power-demand theme: NIPSCO has signed large-load electricity supply agreements with Amazon (ADS), Microsoft and an Alphabet subsidiary, and is building dedicated and pooled generation capacity through its GenCo subsidiary (in which Blackstone holds a minority stake) to serve them.

business_model.summary: NiSource earns substantially all of its income from cost-of-service rate-regulated gas and electric utility operations, where capital invested in infrastructure earns an allowed return set by state regulators (IURC, PUCO, and PA/VA/KY/MD commissions) plus FERC oversight of NIPSCO's transmission tariff. Growth is driven by (1) traditional rate-base growth from safety/modernization capital programs recovered through base rates and trackers (IRP, TDSIC, SAVE, SMRP, GCT, FMCA, CEP, PHMSA IRP), and (2) a newer, commercially-negotiated data-center/large-load business in which NIPSCO and GenCo construct dedicated and pooled generation/transmission assets under long-term (15-20 year) contracts with hyperscale customers, targeting an unlevered IRR greater than NIPSCO's traditional regulated electric return.

revenue_streams.name: Columbia Operations (gas distribution - OH, PA, VA, KY, MD)
NIPSCO Operations - Electric (generation, transmission, distribution + data center contracts)

business_model.customer_type: Regulated B2C/B2B utility customer base (residential, commercial, industrial) plus a small, fast-growing cohort of hyperscale data-center customers (Amazon/ADS, Microsoft, Alphabet subsidiary) under bespoke commercial contracts
business_model.geographic_mix: Six states: Indiana (NIPSCO gas ~0.9m customers, electric ~0.5m customers), Ohio, Pennsylvania, Virginia, Kentucky, Maryland (Columbia gas, ~2.4m customers)

main_competitors: other regulated utilities/munis/co-ops competing for data-center large-load siting
competitive_position.market_position: Exclusive, regulated franchise monopoly within its six-state service territories for gas and electric distribution; in the fast-growing data-center large-load segment, NIPSCO competes nationally and internationally against other utilities and self-generation/behind-the-meter power providers for hyperscaler site selection

moat_factors.description: Exclusive certificated service territories for gas and electric distribution with no retail choice for NIPSCO electric customers in Indiana; competitors cannot duplicate the wires/pipes network
Extensive tracker mechanisms (IRP, TDSIC, SAVE, SMRP, GCT, FMCA, CEP, GCA, FAC) allow near-real-time recovery of capital and commodity costs, reducing regulatory lag and cash-flow risk

moat_factors.factor: First-mover position in northern Indiana data-center corridor
moat_factors.description: Three signed hyperscale contracts (Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet) and a supportive state regulatory/legislative environment for data centers create a land-grab advantage, though this is contestable as other utilities and states compete for the same hyperscaler capital

NIPSCO Holdings II and Generation Holdings II minority stakes bring in third-party equity capital to fund the capital program without diluting common shareholders as much, while preserving investment-grade credit

weaknesses: Customer/industry concentration risk: at full ramp (~2032) NiSource expects ~4,920 MW of capacity dedicated to just three data-center customers, versus ~3,967 MW of current owned generation plus ~1,200 MW of PPAs -- a small number of AI-sector counterparties account for an outsized share of incremental capital

Data-center contract returns are commercially negotiated rather than traditionally rate-regulated, so realized IRR is not guaranteed and is exposed to construction cost overruns, delays, and liquidated-damage provisions

High and rising leverage/equity needs: capital plan has roughly doubled in a year (from $28B to $40B) requiring continuous ATM equity issuance and long-term debt issuance, pressuring credit metrics and diluting existing shareholders

Exposure to an aging coal fleet and federal emergency orders (DOE Section 202(c)) forcing uneconomic coal units (R.M. Schahfer) to keep running, creating execution and cost-recovery uncertainty around the generation transition
Weather-sensitive gas distribution and seasonal cash flows in Columbia Operations

growth_drivers: Data-center/AI large-load strategy: contracts with Amazon (ADS, up to 3,000 MW dispatchable generation), Microsoft (capacity rising to 788 MW by 2031, ~1,100 MW added to the generation pool) and an Alphabet subsidiary, with estimated planned data-center capex of $14.0-14.5 billion and a new 'Pool Resource Assets' model to serve additional large-load customers flexibly

Record base-business capital program: $32 billion of base infrastructure investment planned 2027-2033 (replacement of aging gas mains, electric grid modernization, generation transition) layered on top of $8 billion of GenCo data-center-related capital -- a $40 billion total multi-year plan, up from $28 billion a year earlier

Regulatory tracker mechanisms (IRP, TDSIC, SAVE, SMRP, GCT, FMCA, CEP) that convert capital spending into near-term rate recovery and support management's targeted 6-8% annual base-plan adjusted EPS growth (and higher consolidated growth including GenCo)

Electric generation transition: retirement of remaining coal units (Michigan City by 2028, Schahfer peaking units by 2027) and replacement with renewables, battery storage and new gas-fired peaking/CCGT capacity, some of which also serves data-center load
Potential for additional data-center/hyperscaler contracts beyond the current three, supported by a presently favorable Indiana state regulatory and legislative environment for large-load development

Minority-interest capital partnerships (Blackstone stakes in NIPSCO Holdings II and Generation Holdings II) that bring in third-party capital to help fund the buildout while preserving investment-grade ratings

business.description: Three hyperscale customers will represent a generation capacity commitment larger than NiSource's entire existing fleet; termination, capacity reduction, or AI-capex slowdown by any one of them (e.g., ADS's one-time option to halve committed capacity by 2032) could strand significant invested capital

business.risk: Construction execution on first-of-scale GenCo projects
business.description: Two 1,300 MW CCGTs, 400+100 MW BESS and F-frame CTs are large, novel construction projects with cost-overrun, supply-chain (turbines, transformers, batteries), and schedule risk (CCGT commercial operation date already pushed to 2030 from 2028-2032)
DOE emergency orders have forced continued operation of uneconomic coal units beyond planned retirement dates, creating operational and cost-recovery uncertainty
Other states (NY, TX, PA) have recently imposed data-center moratoria/restrictions; similar measures in Indiana or NIPSCO's territory could delay or impair the data-center strategy

business.risk: Workforce, supply chain and labor availability
business.description: Tight skilled-labor markets and materials/tariff-driven cost inflation could delay the base capital program and the data-center buildout simultaneously

financial.risk: Rapidly escalating capital needs and equity dilution
financial.description: Capital plan grew from $28B to $40B within a year, requiring continuous ATM equity issuance (forward sales at $40-$46/share in 2025-2026) and large debt issuances ($16.2B total debt at YE2025), pressuring per-share growth and credit metrics

NiSource is BBB+/Baa2/BBB (S&P/Moody's/Fitch), investment-grade but with limited headroom; large incremental debt for data-center construction could pressure ratings absent offsetting equity/minority-interest capital

Material reliance on commercial paper, revolving credit and new long-term debt issuance (5.3-6.25% coupons in 2025-2026) exposes financing costs to rate moves during a multi-year capital-intensive buildout

regulatory.risk: IURC approval risk for the ADS, Microsoft and Alphabet contracts and related generation/PPA filings
regulatory.description: Commercial contract terms are subject to regulatory review; disallowance, delay or unfavorable treatment (including ASC 980 regulatory accounting discontinuation in default/termination scenarios) could impair returns

regulatory.risk: Federal GHG/EPA and pipeline-safety rule changes
regulatory.description: Reversal of 2024 Carbon Pollution Standards is currently a tailwind (avoids ~$675m of costs), but policy direction has shifted twice in two years and could reverse again, and PHMSA leak-detection/distribution-pipeline rules remain unsettled

regulatory.risk: State-level gas-electrification and climate policy (e.g., Maryland)
regulatory.description: Maryland regulators are moving toward restricting new gas-main extensions and electrification mandates that could reduce long-run gas demand in Columbia of Maryland

macro.risk: AI capex cycle / hyperscaler demand sensitivity
macro.description: NiSource's data-center growth thesis depends on continued hyperscaler capital spending; a slowdown or re-pricing of AI infrastructure investment (acknowledged explicitly in the Q3-2026 10-Q as a stock-price volatility risk) could reduce demand for additional large-load contracts
Gas distribution revenue (heating season) and electric revenue (cooling season) are weather-sensitive, partially but not fully offset by normalization mechanisms
Gas and power costs are largely tracked and passed through, but rising customer bills from large base-rate capital programs raise affordability and political/regulatory sensitivity

macro_factors.industry_outlook: US regulated gas/electric utilities face a multi-decade grid-modernization and electrification capital cycle; NiSource's footprint additionally sits at the center of the AI-driven data-center electricity demand boom in northern Indiana, a theme expected to continue growing industry-wide, with risk that site-selection competition, equipment lead times, or an AI-capex pullback could slow growth
macro_factors.cyclicality: Low-to-moderate; regulated utility demand is largely non-cyclical, though industrial/commercial gas and electric usage and large-load data-center build-out timing have some sensitivity to broader economic and technology-investment cycles
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: High - heavy reliance on debt and equity issuance to fund an expanding, multi-year $40 billion capital program; allowed ROEs (~9.6-10.0%) and cost of capital are directly linked to rate environment
key_input_costs: Natural gas and coal commodity costs (largely pass-through)
Steel, copper, transformers, turbines and battery storage components (capex inflation/tariff exposure)

recent_developments.event: NIPSCO signed a 20-year electricity supply contract with Microsoft for a northern Indiana data-center campus, capacity rising to 788 MW by 2031, adding roughly 1,100 MW to the GenCo generation pool; third hyperscale customer after Amazon (ADS) and an Alphabet subsidiary

GenCo entered the AGP Tolling Agreement for a 600 MWAC/2,400 MWh third-party-developed battery storage project, and an EPC contract with Quanta for two 239 MW F-frame gas turbines to expand its pooled 'Pool Resource Assets' generation model

Updated capital plan: total 2027-2033 capital investment raised to approximately $40.0 billion ($32.0B base business + $8.0B GenCo/data center), up from the prior $28B (2026-2030) base+ADS estimate disclosed at FY2025 year-end; estimated cost of planned data-center-related expenditures raised to $14.0-14.5 billion
CCGT facility construction timeline for the ADS/GenCo generation project pushed to reach commercial operation during 2030 (from the prior 2028-2032 window) following a change to construction plans

Q3 2026 adjusted EPS of $0.27 beat consensus (~$0.22); revenue of $1.349B grew ~6% YoY but missed consensus; management narrowed FY2026 adjusted EPS guidance to the upper half of the $2.02-$2.07 range

Launched 'Value Captured' multi-year transformation/cost-efficiency program in response to customer affordability concerns, including a Q2 2026 internal reorganization and involuntary employee separations

DOE issued successive 90-day Section 202(c) emergency orders forcing the R.M. Schahfer coal units to keep operating beyond their planned retirement (now through at least December 2026), with cost recovery authorized; NIPSCO's 2026 Integrated Resource Plan process (begun August 2026, expected Q1 2027) is reassessing retirement timelines

ADS Contract (Amazon data-center) executed in September 2025; GenCo 19.9% minority equity interest sold to Blackstone affiliates for ~$35.2M cash plus up to $1.325B of further committed capital; revolving credit facility increased from $1.85B to $2.50B

items.target: $0.30/share quarterly ($1.20 annualized); 2026 increase of ~7.1%; targeted 55-65% payout ratio
items.notes: Management intends to grow the dividend roughly in line with adjusted EPS growth

guidance.management_commentary: Management reiterated that the data-center/GenCo strategy is intended to be accretive and to earn an unlevered return above NIPSCO's traditional regulated electric return, while emphasizing continued execution risk on construction (CCGT commercial operation date pushed to 2030) and financing (ongoing ATM equity issuance and long-term debt issuance) needed to fund the enlarged $40B capital plan without sacrificing investment-grade credit ratings. Management also highlighted the 'Value Captured' cost-efficiency program as a response to customer affordability concerns.

bull_case: First-mover position in the AI/hyperscaler large-load power market with three signed, long-term (15-20 year) contracts (Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet) in a state (Indiana) with a currently supportive regulatory and legislative environment, offering a path to earnings growth well above typical regulated-utility rates

Record, highly visible $40 billion multi-year capital program (2027-2033) with extensive tracker-based cost recovery mechanisms that reduce regulatory lag and support a targeted 6-8% base-plan EPS growth rate, plus incremental GenCo upside
Pure-play regulated gas/electric utility with exclusive franchise territories, stable allowed ROEs (~9.6-10%), and a growing base of rate cases resolved favorably across six states

Minority-interest capital partnerships with Blackstone provide third-party equity funding for the data-center buildout, helping preserve investment-grade credit ratings while reducing common-equity dilution relative to fully self-funding the plan

Data-center contracts are structured to pass savings back to existing retail customers (estimated ~$1.75B in savings), helping offset rate-case and affordability pressure from the base capital program
bear_case: Extreme customer/industry concentration: at full ramp, three hyperscale AI customers are expected to represent generation capacity larger than NiSource's entire current fleet, creating outsized exposure to any slowdown, cancellation, or re-pricing of AI infrastructure capex

Capital plan is escalating faster than disclosed earnings growth can obviously support (nearly 43% increase in multi-year capex in a single year), requiring continuous heavy equity issuance (dilutive ATM/forward sales) and debt issuance that could pressure credit ratings and per-share metrics if execution falters

Construction and financing execution risk on first-of-scale projects (CCGTs, large BESS, F-frame turbines) is high, and the ADS CCGT commercial operation date has already slipped from the original 2028-2032 window to 2030

Returns on data-center contracts are commercially negotiated rather than traditionally cost-of-service regulated, so realized IRR is not guaranteed and is exposed to liquidated damages, cost-overrun sharing, and potential discontinuation of favorable regulatory (ASC 980) accounting treatment in default/termination scenarios

Policy/regulatory whiplash risk: federal GHG and coal-retirement policy has reversed twice in two years (DOE emergency orders forcing coal units to stay open, EPA rule repeals/reinstatements), and some states are now imposing data-center moratoria, raising the risk that the favorable Indiana environment for large loads could tighten
